newsitem.title: USA: U.S. banks seen reporting solid Q2 earnings.
newsitem.headline: U.S. banks seen reporting solid Q2 earnings.

text.p: With help from a buoyant domestic economy, U.S. banks are expected to report year-over-year gains in excess of 10 percent for the second quarter ended June 30.

"The main positives are expense leverage (expenses growing less rapidly than revenues) and continued share repurchases," said Moshe Orenbuch, analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein Co. He said growth in fee income would also contribute to the higher earnings.
Orenbuch expects the banks he tracks to report earnings up 12 percent from a year ago. That would be slightly less than the year-over-year gain in the first quarter of 1997, he said.

"We're looking for another pretty good quarter; it doesn't look a whole lot different than the first quarter," said Sally Pope Davis, analyst at Goldman, Sachs & Co. The analyst expects earnings on average to be up 12 percent year-over-year.
"We're looking for a very good quarter out of NationsBank Corp," Davis said.

She said the Charlotte, N.C.-based giant has enjoyed good revenue growth accompanied by "extremely good expense control." She said NationsBank's integration with Boatmen's Bancshares Inc has gone very smoothly. The $9.8 billion acquisition was completed early in 1997.

A more recent merger, that of Banc One Corp and First USA Inc, is expected to cause some confusion when Banc One reports earnings. The earnings, targeted for July 15, will pool the results of the two companies as if they had been one bank.

Thomas McCandless, analyst at NatWest Securities, said that in effect no one can be sure until the results come out what figure will be used for the prior periods, let alone for the quarter ended June 30.

One exception to the trend of higher earnings is expected to be J.P. Morgan & Co Inc. George Salem, analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison & Co, expects J.P. Morgan to earn $1.72 for the second quarter of 1997, down 16 percent from $2.04 in the first quarter and down 20 percent from $2.14 in the second quarter of 1996.

Salem and other analysts began cutting their J.P. Morgan estimates in early June after they concluded difficult trading conditions in the fixed income markets in April would hurt the company's earnings.

"In sum, bank earnings are still solid and contribute meaningfully to our optimism about the stocks," Salem said in a research note this week. He noted that loan quality "remains stellar," with credit cards the only problem area. Credit card charge-off and delinquency rates are expected to increase and set new highs at many banks, Salem said.

McCandless sounded a note of caution, saying that while the earnings overall look satisfactory, there are signs of slowing beneath the surface. "Our take on the quarter is that it is not as strong as it looks," he said.

He said some banks are booking exceptional profits in areas like foreign exchange, and some banks moved quickly to buy bonds on a market dip earlier this year, locking in high yields. He said those two "drivers to earnings growth do not appear sustainable at the current pace."
For many U.S. banks, earnings per share will get a boost from sizable share repurchase programs.

While some analysts have noted that surging bank stock prices make the repurchases more expensive, some of the bankers have said buybacks are still a good strategy because the stocks still trade at a discount to the Standard & Poor's 500.
